articles.title: In silico conservation and HLA-binding profiles of HMPV F and G protein epitopes: implications for universal vaccine development.
articles.summary: PMID: 42914659. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129282. BackgroundHuman metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a significant cause of respiratory infection, yet no licensed vaccine exists. Variability across viral subgroups, particularly in the attachment (G) protein, can complicate universal design. We assessed the immunogenetic regions in the fusion (F) and G proteins to identify stable vaccine targets.MethodsWe analyzed N = 324 Pittsburgh and N = 655 global HMPV genomes (2017-2022) for genome diversity per viral subgroup. Previously identified epitope sequences were obtained from the Immune Epitope DataBase (IEDB) for F and G proteins and sequence similarity was determined. Using NetMHCpan-4.1, we identified and computed inferred human leukocyte antigen (HLA) binding affinities for 15 epitope variants (1 or 2 substitutions) against universally common human alleles.ResultsThe F protein was highly conserved across all subgroups (>96% amino acid sequence identity). In the G protein, we identified a conserved epitope cluster (G3-G7) where epitope G7 was present in 91% of A2 genomes. Functional modeling of the G-protein epitope variants revealed that the majority of HLA alleles maintained or gained binding affinity, a subset exhibited diminished binding (escape), suggesting these regions are subject to ongoing antigenic drift. B-genotypes showed fewer retained binders and were notably underrepresented in the current epitope databases.ConclusionThe conserved F protein remains an optimal target for neutralization, while the G3-G7 cluster provides a robust secondary target for T-cell mediated immunity. A bivalent vaccine strategy could pair the stable F protein with these high-frequency G-protein epitopes to elicit an immune response. This approach addresses the A2 subgroup, and incorporating B-genotypes through ongoing surveillance and epitope mapping will be essential to achieve comprehensive, multi-antigen coverage across circulating HMPV strains.

articles.title: Safety and immunogenicity of Thailand Government Pharmaceutical Organization (GPO) produced, COVID-19 vaccine, 10 μg HXP-GPOVac: A Phase III, double-blind, randomized trial in comparison with VAXZEVRIA.
articles.summary: PMID: 42869875. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129230. BackgroundHXP-GPOVac is a Thailand-produced, egg-based, inactivated recombinant Newcastle disease virus (NDV)-chimera vaccine expressing a membrane-anchored, prefusion-stabilized SARS-CoV-2 spike (NDV-HXP-S), developed to expand vaccine access. This phase III trial evaluated the safety and immunogenicity of a single HXP-GPOVac dose in healthy or clinically stable Thai adults who had completed a two-dose primary series of an authorized COVID-19 vaccine.MethodsIn this double-blind, randomized, active-controlled trial in Nakhon Phanom, Thailand, 4000 participants were randomized 3:1 to receive HXP-GPOVac or VAXZEVRIA (AstraZeneca, ChAdOx1 nCoV-19). Immunogenicity was assessed by pseudovirus neutralization assay for 50% neutralizing antibody titers (NT50) and ELISA for anti-Spike IgG. Non-inferiority was prespecified for NT50-based endpoints at day 14, defined by (i) a geometric mean concentration (GMC) ratio (HXP-GPOVac/VAXZEVRIA) with 95% CI lower bound >0.67 and (ii) a seroconversion rate (SCR) difference with 95% CI lower bound > -10%.ResultsSolicited AEs occurred in 43.7% of HXP-GPOVac recipients versus 53.5% of VAXZEVRIA recipients (p = 0.01). Most solicited AEs were mild. No vaccine-related serious AEs were reported. At day 14, the NT50 GMC ratio (HXP-GPOVac/VAXZEVRIA) was 0.83 (95% CI lower bound: 0.74), and the SCR difference was -2.35% (95% CI lower bound: -8.72%), both meeting non-inferiority criteria.ConclusionHXP-GPOVac was well-tolerated and demonstrated non-inferior immunogenicity compared with VAXZEVRIA at 14 days after vaccination. articles.title: Cost-effectiveness of universal infant hepatitis B vaccination programme in Finland.
articles.summary: PMID: 42887417. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129171. ObjectivesTo evaluate the cost-effectiveness of a universal infant hepatitis B vaccination programme in Finland.MethodsA static cohort model was employed to compare the health care costs and health effects of a universal infant hepatitis B vaccination programme with the present targeted vaccination programme. Estimates of hepatitis B incidence and hepatitis B-related costs were derived from national register data. The estimated hepatitis B incidence took into account acute asymptomatic infections. An annual discount rate of 3% was applied to costs and health effects and the main outcome measure was cost per quality adjusted life year (QALY) gained. We present the results with different price differences per dose of hexavalent and pentavalent vaccines. Sensitivity analyses identified influential inputs in the cost-effectiveness analysis.ResultsWe estimated 41 acute cases with every fifth being symptomatic, three chronic hepatitis B cases, and three hepatitis B-related deaths in a birth cohort of 58,000 children. The corresponding health care costs were ϵ46,400 and QALYs lost 14.4. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICER) were between ϵ24,500 and ϵ162,900 when the price difference per dose of pentavalent versus hexavalent vaccine was between two and 12 euros. The results were sensitive to hepatitis B incidence, vaccine cost, and discount rate.ConclusionsIn a very low hepatitis B prevalence country such as Finland, a universal infant hepatitis B vaccination programme appears justifiable use of public health care resources only with a very small price difference between pentavalent and hexavalent vaccines.

articles.title: Phase 2 trial to evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of a 25-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (IVT-PCV25) in infants.
articles.summary: PMID: 42906503. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129268. IntroductionIVT-PCV25 is a 25-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine designed to broaden serotype coverage beyond current vaccines. We evaluated the safety and immunogenicity in infants of three dose-ranging formulations of IVT-PCV25 in comparison to licensed Prevnar-20.MethodsIn this double-blind phase 2 trial in the Philippines, 421 healthy infants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) to three IVT-PCV25-formulation arms or a Prevnar-20 arm. Three doses were administered 4-weeks apart from 6 weeks of age, alongside routine vaccinations. Adverse events (AEs), and IgG and functional antibody (opsonophagocytic; OPA) titres were assessed up to 28-days after Dose 3. Unlike IgG concentrations, OPA titres were only measured in a third of the population.ResultsSolicited local and systemic AEs were reported for 90-93% and 94-99% of IVT-PCV25 recipients, respectively, and for 84% and 97% of Prevnar-20 recipients, respectively. These AEs were predominantly mild or moderate, and transient. No serious AE was attributed to IVT-PCV25. All formulations of IVT-PCV25 appeared immunogenic by IgG assay or OPA, or both. IgG GMTs to 19/25 serotype antigens were above the aggregate correlate-of-protection threshold of 0.35 μg/mL; and for the other 6/25 serotypes, the OPA GMTs were > 50-fold the lower limit of quantification (8 dil-1). No clear dose effect was observed. A 2-fold change in antigen quantity only led to a corresponding 2-fold antibody response for four serotypes, and by OPA only. In Prevnar-20 recipients, IgG GMCs were ≥ 0.85 μg/mL for all shared serotypes.ConclusionsIn infants, IVT-PCV25 had an acceptable safety profile. Although the results suggest that IVT-PCV25 has the potential to broaden serotype coverage, there is scope for formulation optimisation by rebalancing serotype-antigen quantities.

articles.title: rVSV-ΔG-EBOV-GP-Nipah-G (also designated PHV02) replication-competent, recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus vaccine for prevention of Nipah virus disease: Standardized template with key considerations for a risk/benefit assessment.
articles.summary: PMID: 42869683. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129113. A recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) expressing the glycoprotein (GP) of Ebola virus (rVSV-EBOV GP) has been approved for preventive immunization against Ebola (Ervebo®, Merck & Co.). The rVSV-EBOV vector was modified to express an additional glycoprotein (G) of Nipah virus (NiV), a bat-borne henipavirus endemic/epidemic in South and Southeast Asia that causes fatal encephalitis and pneumonia. The rVSV-EBOV-GP-NiV G vaccine candidate ("PHV02") is a unique chimeric virus with tropism and immunological properties derived from the wild-type (wt) vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) parent, the rVSV-EBOV-GP vector and the NiV G transgene donor. The EBOV GP enables fusion with the cell membrane and virus entry, whereas the NiV G protein mediates attachment to cells and serves as the antigen for stimulating NiV-specific immunity. This review focuses on the characteristics of the vector and vaccine candidate relevant to clinical and environmental safety, immunogenicity and efficacy. The Brighton Collaboration Benefit-Risk Assessment of VAccines by TechnolOgy (BRAVATO) standardized template is used to update the key characteristics and risks of the rVSV-EBOV vector (previously published [1]) and the novel PHV02 NiV vaccine candidate which is now in clinical trials. The template provides a rich source of information and guide to the supporting literature. While analogies of the PHV02 NiV vaccine to the backbone rVSV-EBOV vector are useful given the more extensive data available on the vector, the template emphasizes that PHV02 is a novel construct from a regulatory perspective and targets a different disease with unique characteristics and pathogenesis. Where similarities and parallels are drawn between nonclinical and clinical outcomes of rVSV-EBOV (vector) and PHV02 (vaccine), the reader should be cognizant of the limitations of these conclusions. The intended use of the standardized template is to provide a cohesive reference allowing vaccine developers and regulatory reviewers to understand characteristics, benefits and risks of a new vaccine candidate against NiV relevant to its future use in human populations, and to compare and contrast these characteristics to an approved vaccine constructed from the same (rVSV) vector system against a different indication (ebolavirus). The systematized template structure should facilitate utility of the paper.

articles.title: Sex differences in human papillomavirus vaccination among Japanese university students and associated factors: a cross-sectional study examining the mediating effect of knowledge and interactions.
articles.summary: PMID: 42913243. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129276. BackgroundHuman papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination rates among Japanese university students, especially among males, remain low. Following the suspension of active recommendations in 2013, vaccination rates have not improved since their resumption in 2022; male vaccination has not been established as a routine.ObjectivesTo describe sex-specific HPV vaccination status and associated factors, examine sex differences in associated patterns, and examine the potential mediating role of HPV-related knowledge.MethodsThis web-based cross-sectional survey was conducted among undergraduates at a Japanese university in April 2025. The data of 3203 participants (1760 males, 1443 females) were analyzed. Self-reported vaccination history was the primary outcome. Multivariable logistic regression, bootstrap-based mediation analysis, and interaction analysis were performed.ResultsThe vaccination rate was 30.1% (3.2% among males vs. 62.9% among females; P < 0.001). Male sex was strongly negatively associated with vaccination (OR = 0.024; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.017-0.034). Knowledge of free vaccination (OR = 3.477) and HPV-related diseases (OR = 1.758) showed positive associations. In females, only knowledge variables were significant, whereas in males, lifestyle variables were also associated. The indirect effect of sex on vaccination via HPV-related knowledge was statistically significant (indirect effect β = -0.263; 95% CI: -0.383 to -0.141), indicating partial mediation. Among unvaccinated males, 81.1% reported not needing the vaccine; 50.4% of unvaccinated females cited concerns about adverse effects.ConclusionsLegislation mandating routine vaccination for males, subsidized costs, parental education, and sex-specific university-based programs are needed.

articles.title: Waning immunity, an age shift, and rising adult burden of varicella after two decades of single-dose vaccination in South Korea.
articles.summary: PMID: 42879902. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129240. BackgroundMany countries have not adopted universal varicella vaccination (UVV), citing concerns that it could shift disease burden toward older, higher-risk age groups and be insufficiently cost-effective. Long-term data under sustained single-dose vaccination remain scarce. We assessed the immunological, epidemiological, and healthcare cost consequences of two decades of South Korea's single-dose National Immunization Program, which has maintained >95% coverage since 2005 without the anticipated decline in incidence.MethodsWe analyzed varicella-zoster virus immunoglobulin G titers in 3765 healthcare personnel (HCP) by birth group. We also examined national surveillance (Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency) and insurance claims (Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service) data from 2010 to 2024.ResultsSeronegativity was highest among HCP born during 1990-1994 (adjusted odds ratio, 3.83), and geometric mean titers declined across successive birth groups (geometric mean ratio, 0.70 [95% confidence interval, 0.63-0.77], 2000-2004 vs. pre-1980), indicating waning immunity. In 2024, adolescents surpassed children aged <10 years as the largest proportion of cases for the first time. Age-specific incidence rates increased approximately ninefold in adolescents and threefold in adults while remaining unchanged in children. Among adults, the proportion of varicella meningitis cases rose from 16.4% to 72.9%, and their share of varicella-related healthcare costs rose from 21.2% to 41.9%.ConclusionsAfter two decades of sustained high single-dose coverage, these findings provide evidence relevant to concerns about age shift and disease severity in settings yet to adopt UVV and support reassessment of the single-dose schedule.

articles.title: Ischemic stroke after bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination and influenza vaccination during the 2022-2023 season: a multi-site self-controlled case series study.
articles.summary: PMID: 42914658. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129263. BackgroundThe Vaccine Safety Datalink (VSD) detected a statistical signal for ischemic events (ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack) following bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination through prospective surveillance during 2022-2023. Although multiple studies from other surveillance systems and countries reported no increased risk, important methodological limitations remained. This U.S. study addressed those limitations by evaluating the ischemic stroke risk following bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination, influenza vaccination, and their same-day coadministration using an event-dependent self-controlled case series (SCCS) design.MethodsStudy outcomes included first-ever ischemic stroke (primary outcome), first-in-1-year ischemic stroke (secondary outcome), and ischemic events (exploratory outcomes), identified using ICD-10-CM codes in inpatient and emergency department settings during September 1, 2022-March 31, 2023, among individuals aged ≥12 years across eight VSD sites. Analyses were conducted separately for Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna bivalent vaccines, with relative incidences (RI) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) estimated for 1-21-day and 1-42-day risk intervals, using person-time outside these intervals as the control period. Subgroup analyses were performed by age group (12-64, ≥65 years) and history of documented SARS-CoV-2 infection.ResultsA total of 6510 first-ever ischemic strokes were identified among more than 6.8 million participants. Among recipients of Pfizer-BioNTech bivalent COVID-19 and influenza vaccines, no statistically significant increased risk of first-ever ischemic stroke was observed following bivalent COVID-19 vaccination (RI = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.63-1.41), influenza vaccination (RI = 0.95; 95% CI: 0.82-1.10), or same-day coadministration (RI = 1.15; 95% CI: 0.88-1.49) within 1-21-day risk intervals; findings were similar for 1-42-day intervals. Comparable null results were observed for Moderna vaccine and across all subgroups, secondary, and exploratory outcomes.ConclusionNo increased risk of ischemic stroke was found following bivalent mRNA COVID-19 vaccination, influenza vaccination, or their coadministration in this multi-site SCCS study. These findings are consistent with previous studies and underscore the importance of continued vaccine safety monitoring.

articles.title: Understanding rotavirus vaccine acceptance in Indonesia: a WHO BeSD-based exploration of parents' and religious leaders' perspectives in three provinces.
articles.summary: PMID: 42879900. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129211. BackgroundDisparities in rotavirus vaccine uptake in Indonesia persist despite its national implementation, yet, the community-level determinants of vaccination remain underexplored. Understanding the behavioural and social factors influencing vaccination decisions is essential for developing interventions that improve vaccine uptake in the community.MethodsA qualitative study was conducted using the World Health Organization Behavioural and Social Drivers (WHO BeSD) framework. Data were collected between May and December 2025 through five focus group discussions and 24 in-depth interviews with parents and religious leaders in Yogyakarta, Bali, and the Moluccas. Participants were purposively sampled to capture diverse experiences and perspectives. Data were analysed using a deductive thematic approach guided by the four BeSD domains: Thinking and Feeling, Social Processes, Motivation, and Practical Issues.ResultsSeventy-one participants (61 parents and 10 religious leaders) took part in the study. Overall acceptance of rotavirus vaccination was high and driven by trust in vaccine benefits and confidence in health services. Within the Thinking and Feeling domain, participants recognised the severity of diarrhoeal disease and the protective value of vaccination, although concerns about adverse effects and limited access to information remained, particularly in rural areas. Social Processes generally supported vaccine uptake through health workers' recommendations, community endorsement, and support from religious leaders. Most mothers reported autonomy in vaccination decision-making, although gender-related influences persisted in some households. Motivation to vaccinate was strengthened by the desire to protect children from severe illness. Under Practical Issues, participants described vaccination services as accessible through primary healthcare facilities but highlighted the need for improved information dissemination and more reliable vaccine availability in remote areas.ConclusionsImproving vaccine literacy, strengthening service delivery, and addressing practical barriers are critical to increasing complete rotavirus vaccination uptake. Tailored communication and engagement of parents, religious leaders, and community stakeholders may further enhance vaccine acceptance and uptake across diverse Indonesian settings.

articles.title: Protection of Omicron XBB.1.5 vaccine, previous infection, and their induced neutralizing antibodies against symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection during Omicron KP.3 wave.
articles.summary: PMID: 42879903. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129242. articles.title: When models diverge: Harmonizing pneumococcal vaccination cost-effectiveness analyses to inform PCV20 and PCV21 use in US adults.
articles.summary: PMID: 42892161. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129267. ObjectivesPolicymakers use decision models to assess pneumococcal vaccine cost-effectiveness, but different models often yield inconsistent results. Other analyses compared differing cohort structures and vaccine timing.ResultsInitial results diverged widely, driven by differing disease risk, vaccination likelihood and serotype coverage, and childhood vaccination indirect effects - all uncertain and debated. Cost-effectiveness ratios were very sensitive to alternative model inputs. Model comparisons can identify uncertainty, reveal evidence gaps, enhance transparency, and potentially improve decision making.

articles.title: Cross-protection and type-replacement over the 17 years after human papillomavirus vaccine introduction in young women.
articles.summary: PMID: 42901130. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129244. BackgroundThe study aim was to examine trends in non-4-valent and non-9-valent vaccine-type HPV detection over the first 17 years after U.S. HPV vaccine introduction among young women.MethodsWe recruited 13-26 year-old sexually experienced women (N = 2335) from hospital and community clinics for six surveillance studies from 2006 to 2023, with testing for HPV DNA by Roche Linear Array or TypeSeq2. Outcome variables were: 1) potentially carcinogenic alpha-9 and -7 non-vaccine-type HPV genetically related to HPV16 or 18 but not targeted by the 4- or 9-valent vaccines (to assess for cross-protection) and 2) potentially carcinogenic alpha-5, -6, and - 11 non-vaccine-type HPV not closely genetically related to types targeted by the 4- or 9-valent vaccines (to assess for type replacement). We used inverse probability of treatment weighting with propensity score to balance between-wave differences in participant characteristics in prevalence estimates and in tests of linear trend using surveillance study as a continuous variable.ResultsAmong all, vaccinated, and unvaccinated participants, there were no significant trends in the prevalence of at least 1 non-vaccine-type HPV genetically related to HPV16 and/or HPV18 but not targeted by the 4- or 9-valent vaccines. Positivity for non-vaccine-type HPV genetically unrelated to types targeted by the 4- or 9-valent vaccines remained stable from 2006 to 2015 but increased from 2016 to 2023; the trend was significant for all groups.ConclusionsWe did not find evidence for cross-protection against types not targeted by the 4-valent or 9-valent vaccines, but did find a signal for possible emerging type replacement.

articles.title: High willingness to receive a vaccine for gonorrhoea prevention among gay, bisexual, queer, and other sexuality diverse men, and non-binary people in Australia.
articles.summary: PMID: 42869876. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129233. Gonorrhoea incidence and antimicrobial resistance are increasing among gay, bisexual, queer, and other sexuality diverse men, and non-binary (GBQ+) people. Observational studies suggested that 4CMenB vaccine (Bexsero®) may provide partial protection against gonorrhoea, but recent randomised trials found no clear evidence of protection. We analysed willingness to receive 4CMenB for gonorrhoea prevention in a 2025 Australian cross-sectional survey of GBQ+ individuals aged ≥16 years. Multivariable logistic regression examined associated factors. Among 2138 participants (median age 39 years), 89.2% were willing to be vaccinated. Willingness was lower among participants aged ≥30 (aOR = 0.46;95%CI = 0.29-0.74), born outside Australia (aOR = 0.71;95%CI = 0.51-0.99), higher among those reporting recent HIV PrEP use (aOR = 2.80;95%CI = 1.30-5.99), familiarity with antimicrobial resistance (aOR = 2.26;95%CI = 1.61-3.18), and willingness to take an antibiotic pill after sex to prevent STIs (aOR = 5.42;95%CI = 3.85-7.61). Willingness was high and aligned more with prevention engagement and biomedical prevention attitudes than with sexual risk behaviours, suggesting future gonorrhoea vaccines may be acceptable in this population.

articles.title: Development and analytical characterization of a 24-plex microsphere-based assay for the quantitation of the antibodies against pneumococcal vaccine serotypes.
articles.summary: PMID: 42906504. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129266. BackgroundQuantitative assessment of pneumococcal vaccine-induced immunity is essential for monitoring vaccine effectiveness. The World Health Organization (WHO) pneumococcal polysaccharide enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (Pn PS ELISA) remains the reference standard for measuring serotype-specific IgG concentrations; however, it is limited by its low throughput and high resource requirements. Our study aim is to develop and analytically characterize a 24-plex microsphere-based immunoassay for simultaneous quantitation of serotype-specific IgG antibodies against 24 pneumococcal vaccine serotypes.MethodsPneumococcal polysaccharides were conjugated to magnetic microspheres using the DMTMM (4-(4,6-dimethoxy-1,3,5-triazin-2-yl)-4-methyl-morpholinium chloride) coupling method, and assay performance was evaluated using the WHO reference serum (007sp).ResultsThe 24-plex assay demonstrated assay working ranges with lower limits of quantitation between 0.4 and 6.7 ng/mL and upper limits up to 38,699 ng/mL. Homologous inhibition exceeded 80% across all serotypes, while heterologous inhibition remained below 20% except for structurally related serogroups (6A/6B, 9N/9V, 19A/19F). Intra- and inter-assay precision met the predefined acceptance criterion of coefficients of variation below 20% for all serotypes, and accuracy ranged between 87% and 118%. Concentration-based comparison with the WHO Pn PS ELISA using Deming regression showed slopes close to unity for most serotypes, indicating quantitative consistency between the two assays within the evaluated reference-serum dilution series.ConclusionOur multiplex assay covers 24 pneumococcal vaccine serotypes supporting its analytical performance and comparability with WHO Pn PS ELISA. Our 24-plex assay provides a high-throughput and efficient method for pneumococcal serotype-specific IgG quantification, while further clinical and inter-laboratory evaluation is warranted.

articles.title: Quantifying the impact of pathogen interactions on vaccine effectiveness estimates in the test-negative design.
articles.summary: PMID: 42901129. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129265. The test-negative design (TND) has been widely adopted for real-world vaccine effectiveness (VE) assessment, assuming that control selection is independent of vaccination status. However, pathogen interactions may contradict this assumption, posing challenges to VE evaluations. We developed a theoretical framework to quantify the pathogen-dependence-related biases in VE estimates. The framework was further empirically evaluated using data from 66,117 pediatric patients tested for multiple respiratory pathogens during 2023-2024, comparing influenza VE estimates using standard influenza-negative controls with those using specific non-influenza pathogen positive or negative controls. The theoretical framework indicated that the TND may overestimate VE even without pathogen dependence. Pathogen dependence further modified influenza VE estimates in a pathogen-specific direction, i.e., positive pathogen dependence with influenza tended to overestimate influenza VE, whereas negative pathogen dependence biased VE estimates downward. However, the magnitude of dependence-related bias was generally smaller than the bias attributable to the baseline model-specific discrepancy. The use of all-pathogen-negative controls minimized estimation bias. These findings suggest that pathogen dependence and control selection should be considered when using TND for VE estimation.
articles.normalizedTitle: Quantifying the impact of pathogen interactions on vaccine effectiveness estimates in the test-negative design.

articles.title: Timeliness of routine childhood vaccination in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: data from national vaccine surveys in 2021/2022, 2023 and 2024.
articles.summary: PMID: 42892160. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129222. BackgroundWhile crude vaccine coverage is a frequently reported coverage measure in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), timeliness of vaccine delivery is comparatively understudied. To achieve full vaccine benefits, both high coverage and timely delivery are required. This analysis investigated the timeliness of childhood vaccinations and associated factors across three national Vaccine Coverage Surveys conducted in 2021/2022, 2023, and 2024 in the DRC.MethodsWe conducted a secondary analysis of vaccination coverage data from 79,761 children aged 12-23 months. Weighted coverages and timeliness among vaccinated children were determined. Time-to-event analyses using Kaplan-Meier curves and multilevel Cox regression models were used to assess trends and predictors of vaccination timeliness.ResultsNationally, crude estimates of complete vaccination coverage were 50.1% (48.5-51.7) in 2021/2022, 55.1% (53.6-56.6) in 2023 and 38.4% (37.1-39.6) in 2024, with timely administration among vaccinated individuals ranging from 17.5% to 51.8%. Timely complete vaccination significantly decreased over time from 23.4% (22.0-24.8) in 2021/2022 to 17.5% (16.6-18.5) in 2024 with substantial variance among provinces and health zones. Children whose mothers/guardians had good knowledge about vaccine preventable diseases (VPDs) were consistently more likely to receive timely vaccines across surveys (aHR = 1.16 (1.08-1.25); aHR = 1.09 (1.02-1.15); aHR = 1.10 (1.02-1.14)) respectively in 2021/2022, 2023 and 2024; while crowded households (with three or more children under five) showed delayed vaccination in 2021/2022 and 2023 (aHR = 0.86 (0.77-0.97); aHR = 0.89 (0.81-0.99) respectively). In 2021/2022, households who reported paying for a vaccination card, or home-based records also reported higher rates of delayed vaccination completion (aHR = 0.87, p = 0.011).ConclusionTimeliness among vaccinated children has declined over time, with data showing worsening trends across three successive survey years. Addressing regional disparities, improving caregiver's health education, and removing financial barriers are essential to enhance coverage and timeliness in childhood immunization.

articles.title: Purpose in life and shingles vaccination and infection.
articles.summary: PMID: 42879901. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129243. Purpose in life is a positive psychological resource associated with preventive behavior and better health outcomes in older adulthood. This study examines whether purpose is associated with likelihood of getting vaccinated against shingles and likelihood of having had shingles. Participants in the Health and Retirement Study (N = 14,066; Mage = 68.13, SD = 10.29) reported on their purpose in life. Vaccine uptake and having had shingles was aggregated across eight waves from 2008 to 2022. Every standard deviation of purpose was associated with a 16% higher likelihood of having received the shingles vaccine (OR = 1.16, 95% CI = 1.12-1.20). This association was independent of depressive symptoms and did not vary by sex, race, ethnicity, or education. The association was slightly stronger among relatively older adults, perhaps because the recommended age of vaccination changed during the study period. Purpose was unrelated to having had shingles. Leveraging purpose in life could be a promising target to increase uptake of the shingles vaccine.

articles.title: Comparing two case definitions for including severe acute respiratory infection patients in influenza and COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness studies among older adults using the test-negative design: VEBIS hospital network, seven European countries, 2023/24.
articles.summary: PMID: 42869874. DOI: 10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129234. IntroductionTwo severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) case definitions (CDs) are often used in test-negative design (TND) hospital-based vaccine effectiveness (VE) studies. SARI-CD1 requires ≥1 symptom (cough, fever, shortness of breath, anosmia, ageusia, or dysgeusia); SARI-CD2 requires both fever and cough. Using VEBIS hospital network end-of-season 2023/24 data, we compared the effect of these CDs on influenza and COVID-19 VE estimates in Europe.MethodsUsing the TND, we restricted analysis to seven countries recruiting patients using SARI-CD1; we created a subset of SARI patients also meeting SARI-CD2. Cases were RT-PCR-positive for influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), or SARS-CoV-2; controls were influenza or SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR-negative. We estimated VE among patients ≥65 years using logistic regression adjusted for country, onset date, age, sex, and chronic conditions. We estimated VE overall, by age group (65-79, ≥80 years) and time since vaccination (14-59, 60-119, ≥120 days). Absolute VE differences ≥10% were considered relevant.ResultsPatient characteristics and outcomes were similar across CDs. SARI-CD1 had slightly more vaccinated cases, with little difference in controls between the two CDs. For influenza, the absolute VE difference between SARI-CD1 and SARI-CD2 was 10% for influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 (34% vs 44%), 19% among those aged ≥80 years (21% vs 40%) and 18% at 60-119 days post-vaccination (4% vs 22%). For SARS-CoV-2, absolute VE differences were 11% overall (29% vs 40%), 11% among ≥80 years (33% vs 44%), and 12% at 60-119 days (34% vs 46%). All other absolute VE differences were < 10%.ConclusionsVE was similar for influenza A(H3N2), adults 65-79 years and 14-60 days post-vaccination. We observed signals of higher VE with SARI-CD2 for influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 and SARS-CoV-2, particularly among adults ≥80 years and ≥ 60 days post-vaccination, although 95% CIs overlapped. These signals suggest CDs may contribute to VE variability and VE studies should clearly indicate CDs used.
